newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, Belarus commemorate Bolshevik revolution.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, Belarus commemorate Bolshevik revolution.

text.p: Thousands of Ukrainian Communists marked the anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution on Thursday while nationalists showed their contempt for the former Soviet Union by celebrating their independence from it.
Up to 6,000 mostly elderly people marched through central Kiev chanting slogans against President Leonid Kuchma. "Reforms, Kuchma -- the people have perished!" they shouted.
The elderly have suffered most under market reforms introduced after Ukraine broke free of the Kremlin in 1991.
The crowd rallied outside an exhibition hall, once a museum to Soviet founder Vladimir Lenin but now home to enterprises like "Exquisite", one of Kiev's most expensive restaurants.
A crowd of pensioners gathered around the only big Lenin statue left in Kiev, placed flowers at his feet and complained of monthly allowances as low as the equivalent of $20.
Meanwhile about 4,000 nationalists, waving blue and yellow Ukrainian flags, gathered outside the 11th century St Sofia cathedral where mass pro-independence rallies were held in 1991.
They began their march at a statue to Taras Shevchenko, the 19th century poet who symbolises Ukrainian culture and language.
Ultra-nationalists rallied under the red and black banner of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army -- UPA -- which fought both Adolf Hitler's Nazi forces and Soviet troops during World War Two.

The largest of the communist rallies elsewhere in Ukraine was in the southeastern industrial city of Donetsk, where Interfax-Ukraine news agency said about 10,000 people protested at Kuchma's policies and demanded his resignation.
In Minsk, the capital of the neighbouring former Soviet republic of Belarus, about 5,000 people rallied in Gorky Park.
They were split between supporters of President Alexander Lukashenko, who approve of his policy of forming a union with Russia, and opponents who accuse him of building a dictatorship.
"Only a dictatorship of the proletariat can lead to socialism!" read one banner.
Lukashenko, whose rule has become increasingly authoritarian since he won a landslide victory in July 1994, is locked in a battle with parliament and the constitutional court.
They are trying to stop him enforcing a referendum scheduled for November 24 to extend his term and broaden his powers.
